blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
pivot_longer(), from the tidyr package, makes a data frame longer: it turns a set of columns into two, one holding the old column names and one holding their values, and repeats the other columns. It increases the rows and decreases the columns. pivot_wider() does the reverse.

A key is a column, or set of columns, whose values pick out the row they belong to. A join combines two data frames, x and y, by matching rows whose keys are equal. left_join(x, y), from the dplyr package, keeps every row of x and adds the columns of y. A row of x with no match in y gets NA in the new columns. A row of x that matches several rows of y appears once for each match. anti_join(x, y) returns the rows of x that have no match in y.

by names the key.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
The wide table. A clinic writes a patient’s weight at three visits in three columns: visit 1, visit 2, visit 3. But “visit” is a variable, and here its values sit in the column names. In the column names, summarise(.by = visit) cannot reach them.

pivot_longer() turns the three columns into two: one saying which visit, one saying the weight.

The two files. A survey sends the demographics in one file and the measurements in another, with a participant number in both.

Here is the trap with joins. Suppose a key appears twice in the second file, by a slip in data entry. Then the matching row of the first file appears twice in the result. No error, no warning.

So count the rows before and after every join. Find keys that appear more than once. Find rows that did not match with anti_join().

blocks.alt: A bar chart of four counts: body measures file 8860, demographics file 11933, joined file 8860, demographic rows with no match 3073.
blocks.caption: Rows in the two NHANES 2021–2023 files and in their join on SEQN. The body measures file has 8860 rows and the demographics file 11933. The left join of body measures to demographics keeps 8860, and the 3073 demographic rows with no body measures are participants who were interviewed but not examined. These are counts of rows, not survey estimates.

blocks.alt: A line chart over visits 1 to 3. Patient 101: 82.4, 80.9, 79.5 kg. Patient 102: 95, 93.2, 92.8 kg. Mean of the weights recorded: 84.8, 87.1, 82.4 kg, rising at visit 2. Patient 103, weighed only at visits 1 and 3, is not drawn.
blocks.caption: Weights in the made-up register at visits 1, 2 and 3, after pivot_longer() made the visit a column. Patients 101 and 102 lose weight at every visit, yet the mean of the weights recorded rises from 84.8 kg at visit 1 to 87.1 kg at visit 2, then falls to 82.4 kg. Visit 2 has 2 weights, not 3: patient 103, the lightest (77.1 kg at visit 1, 75 kg at visit 3), was not weighed there and has no line here, so the visit 2 mean is a mean of different people.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a made-up weight register in the wide shape a clinic would write by hand. Each patient’s weight in kilograms at three visits sits in three columns. Patient 103 missed visit 2.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tidyr)

weights_wide <- tibble(
  id = c(101, 102, 103),
  weight_v1 = c(82.4, 95.0, 77.1),
  weight_v2 = c(80.9, 93.2, NA),
  weight_v3 = c(79.5, 92.8, 75.0)
)

Try to get the mean weight at each visit. The visit number is not in any column. It is part of three column names, so there is nothing to group by. You could write three mean() calls, one per column, and a fourth when a visit is added. Instead, make the visit a column:

weights_long <- weights_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("weight_v"),
    names_to = "visit",
    names_prefix = "weight_v",
    values_to = "weight_kg"
  )

weights_long
# A tibble: 9 × 3
     id visit weight_kg
  <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
1   101 1          82.4
2   101 2          80.9
3   101 3          79.5
4   102 1          95
5   102 2          93.2
6   102 3          92.8
7   103 1          77.1
8   103 2          NA
9   103 3          75

Read the arguments in order. cols names the three columns to fold. names_to names the new column that receives their names. names_prefix takes “weight_v” off the front, so the visit column holds 1, 2 and 3. values_to names the column that receives the weights.

Three patients times three visits is nine rows. Each row is one patient at one visit, which is what one observation is here. Patient 103’s missing visit 2 is a row with NA, not a gap. Now the visit is a column, and the last section’s tools work:

weights_long |>
  summarise(
    n_weights = sum(!is.na(weight_kg)),
    mean_kg = mean(weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = visit
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  visit n_weights mean_kg
  <chr>     <int>   <dbl>
1 1             3    84.8
2 2             2    87.1
3 3             3    82.4

Look at the means: 84.8, 87.1, 82.4. The mean went up at visit 2, though every patient weighed there lost weight. The count explains it. Visit 2 has 2 weights, not 3: the lightest patient was missing, so the visit 2 mean is a mean of two different people. A mean over visits compares visits only when the same people are in every visit. The count beside the mean is how you see that.

For the printed table, turn it back:

weights_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = visit,
    values_from = weight_kg,
    names_prefix = "weight_v"
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 4
     id weight_v1 weight_v2 weight_v3
  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1   101      82.4      80.9      79.5
2   102      95        93.2      92.8
3   103      77.1      NA        75

The same three rows and four columns you started with. names_from names the column whose values become the new column names, and values_from the column that fills them. The remaining columns, here id, pick out the rows. values_fill = 0 puts 0 where a combination has no value; use it only for counts. Long for working, wide for reading.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The three patients are made up. Their weights show the reshaping and say nothing about any treatment or any person.

pivot_longer() is right only when the folded columns hold the same variable in the same unit. Folding a weight column and a height column into one value column would make a column with two units in it. The tools would compute a mean of it without complaint.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now two files. A made-up clinic keeps demographics in one table and BMI in another, with the patient number id in both. Patient 102 was entered twice in the demographics table, by a slip at the registration desk. Patient 106 has a BMI and no demographic record.

demographics <- tibble(
  id = c(101, 102, 102, 103, 104, 105),
  sex = c("F", "M", "M", "F", "M", "F"),
  age = c(34, 51, 51, 45, 29, 60)
)

bmi <- tibble(
  id = c(101, 102, 103, 105, 106),
  bmi = c(27.1, 31.4, 24.9, 29.8, 22.3)
)

nrow(bmi)

bmi_demo <- bmi |>
  left_join(demographics, by = "id")

nrow(bmi_demo)
bmi_demo
[1] 5
[1] 6
# A tibble: 6 × 4
     id   bmi sex     age
  <dbl> <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
1   101  27.1 F        34
2   102  31.4 M        51
3   102  31.4 M        51
4   103  24.9 F        45
5   105  29.8 F        60
6   106  22.3 <NA>     NA

Five rows went in and six came out. Patient 102 is there twice, because the key 102 matched two rows of demographics. R printed no warning. Every later count and mean would include patient 102 twice, and a summary of 6 BMIs would be reported for 5 patients.

Patient 106 is there once, with NA for sex and age. left_join() kept the row, because it keeps every row of the first table, and had nothing to fill in.

Three lines find both problems. Count each key, and keep any that appear more than once. Then ask which BMI rows have no partner:

demographics |>
  count(id) |>
  filter(n > 1)

bmi |>
  anti_join(demographics, by = "id")
# A tibble: 1 × 2
     id     n
  <dbl> <int>
1   102     2
# A tibble: 1 × 2
     id   bmi
  <dbl> <dbl>
1   106  22.3

Key 102 appears twice. Patient 106 has no demographic record. Neither is fixed by editing the raw file. Patient 106’s missing record is a question for the clinic. The duplicate is removed by a line of code, with a comment saying why; a later section shows how to make the script stop on it.

Last, make the join refuse to add rows. The relationship argument states how many matches each row is expected to have, and the join stops with an error if the data break it. Each BMI row should match at most one row of demographics, which relationship = "many-to-one" says:

bmi |>
  left_join(demographics, by = "id", relationship = "many-to-one")
Error in `left_join()`:
! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`.
ℹ Row 2 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.

Now the script stops at the join and names the row that broke the rule, instead of carrying a wrong count into every table after it.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The register is made up, and its five patients describe nobody.

A duplicated key is not always an error. A table of visits has one row per visit, so a patient with three visits has the same id three times, and joining demographics to it should repeat each patient’s age three times. The question is never “are there repeats?” but “should there be?”, and the answer comes from what one row stands for.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Now the real case. NHANES, the American survey whose body measures file you read in the section on raw files, sends its demographics in a second file. Both files carry SEQN, the participant’s sequence number. Read both, keep a few columns of each, and count rows before and after the join.

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

nrow(bmx)
nrow(demo)

body <- bmx |>
  select(SEQN, BMXWT, BMXHT, BMXBMI) |>
  left_join(
    demo |> select(SEQN, RIDSTATR, RIAGENDR, RIDAGEYR),
    by = "SEQN",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

nrow(body)
[1] 8860
[1] 11933
[1] 8860

The body measures file has 8860 rows and the demographics file 11933. The join kept 8860, the same as went in. relationship = "one-to-one" expects each key at most once on each side; it did not stop, so no SEQN appears twice in either file.

The demographics file has 3073 more rows than the body measures file. Who are they? Ask which demographic rows found no body measures, and look at their RIDSTATR. The codebook says that column records whether a participant was interviewed and examined, or only interviewed.

bmx |>
  anti_join(demo, by = "SEQN") |>
  nrow()

demo |>
  anti_join(bmx, by = "SEQN") |>
  count(RIDSTATR)
[1] 0
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  RIDSTATR     n
     <dbl> <int>
1        1  3073

Every body-measures row found its demographics: 0 failed to match. The 3073 demographic rows with no body measures all have RIDSTATR 1. In the codebook’s words, they were only interviewed, and never examined, so there was nothing to measure. The two counts agree:

11933 - 8860 = 3073

Table Rows
body measures 8860
demographics 11933
joined 8860
demographics, no match 3073

Now the joined table can answer a question neither file could alone. How many adults aged 20 or over have a body measures record, and what is their BMI, by the codebook’s RIAGENDR, where 1 is male and 2 is female?

body |>
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_bmi = sum(!is.na(BMXBMI)),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMXBMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bmi = median(BMXBMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = RIAGENDR
  )
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  RIAGENDR n_rows n_bmi mean_bmi median_bmi
     <dbl>  <int> <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>
1        1   2720  2680     29.3       28.1
2        2   3344  3290     30.3       28.7

2720 men and 3344 women, 6064 adults in all, of whom 2680 and 3290 have a BMI. Their mean BMI is 29.3 and 30.3 kg/m2, and the medians are 28.1 and 28.7 kg/m2.

These are the mean and median of the rows in the file, unweighted. The survey’s documentation says its sample weights should be used to analyse these data. Without them, these numbers describe the people examined, and estimate nothing about adults in the United States. The book on survey data teaches the weights.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
A join on a key is also the core of a database query; the next rung writes the same joins in SQL (Structured Query Language).

The join worked cleanly because NHANES built both files around one key and published it. A thesis dataset with a register typed in one place and laboratory results in another rarely has a key that clean: names spelled two ways, IDs with and without a leading zero. The checks are the same; expect them to find more.

The adult summary includes everyone aged 20 or over who was examined. It does not exclude anyone for whom BMI means something different, such as women who were pregnant at the examination. A real analysis would decide that, in code, before summarising, as the last section of this book does.

points.html: Count the rows before and after every join. A left_join() that returns more rows than went in has found a key that appears more than once in the second table. It says nothing about it.
The error is to think a join only adds columns. It also adds rows when a key repeats, and every count and mean after it counts those rows again.
Before a join, check the key in each table: count each value with count() and keep those with n > 1.

Always write by. Left out, the join matches on every column the two tables share by name. A column called year or date may mean different things in each. It will then be matched too. dplyr names the columns it used in a message that is easy to miss.
When a wide table has values of a variable in its column names, make it long with pivot_longer() before summarising.
A mean at each visit compares visits only if the same people are in every visit. Print the count at each visit.
When a trainee’s merged thesis file “has a few more rows than it should”, do not let them delete rows by hand.
The join checks can tell you that keys match and how often. They cannot tell you that two rows with the same key are really the same person.

blocks.prompt: Add to a script the join of the NHANES body measures file to the demographics file on SEQN. Print five counts: the rows of each file, the rows of the result, the body-measures rows with no demographics, and the joined rows with an age of 20 or over. State what each count tells you.
blocks.answer:
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

body <- bmx |>
  left_join(demo, by = "SEQN", relationship = "one-to-one")

nrow(bmx)
nrow(demo)
nrow(body)
nrow(anti_join(bmx, demo, by = "SEQN"))
nrow(filter(body, RIDAGEYR >= 20))
[1] 8860
[1] 11933
[1] 8860
[1] 0
[1] 6064

8860 rows of body measures and 11933 of demographics. The join has 8860 rows: none was added, and relationship = "one-to-one" confirms no key repeats. No body measures row lacks demographics. 6064 joined rows are adults aged 20 or over. Every count is of rows in the files; none is a survey estimate.

blocks.prompt: A colleague merged her thesis questionnaire file with the laboratory results in a spreadsheet. She sorted both by participant ID, pasted the laboratory columns beside the questionnaire columns, and saved the result as a new file. Say what can go wrong, and how to do it in code.
blocks.answer:
Pasting side by side matches rows by position, not by ID. It is right only if both files hold exactly the same participants, each exactly once, sorted the same way. One participant missing from the laboratory file, or entered twice, shifts every row below by one. Every participant below the slip then carries someone else’s results, and nothing in the file shows it.

The merged file also has no record of how it was made. Nobody can redo the step and check it.

Do it in code instead, in four steps.

  1. Read both raw files, and count each ID in each with count(id) |> filter(n > 1).
  2. Join with left_join(questionnaire, lab, by = "id", relationship = "one-to-one").
  3. Compare the row counts before and after.
  4. List the unmatched participants with anti_join(), both ways round.

The raw files stay as they arrived. The merge reruns whenever either file changes.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, say what each of these returns: pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), left_join(x, y) and anti_join(x, y).
blocks.answer:
What each returns:

  • pivot_longer(): the same data with more rows and fewer columns; a set of columns becomes a column of their names and a column of their values.
  • pivot_wider(): the reverse, with fewer rows and more columns.
  • left_join(x, y): every row of x, with the columns of y added where the keys match; NA where they do not; a row repeated when its key matches several rows of y.
  • anti_join(x, y): only the rows of x whose key has no match in y.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up table:

library(tidyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

screen <- tibble(child = "A", height_2024 = 121, height_2025 = 127)

Make it long, with a column year and a column height_cm. How many rows will it have?
blocks.answer:
screen |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("height_"),
    names_to = "year",
    names_prefix = "height_",
    values_to = "height_cm"
  )
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  child year  height_cm
  <chr> <chr>     <dbl>
1 A     2024        121
2 A     2025        127

Two rows: one child, two years. The year column holds text, “2024” and “2025”, because it came from column names.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up long table:

library(tidyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

long <- tibble(
  district = c("Durg", "Durg", "Korba", "Korba"),
  round = c("r1", "r2", "r1", "r2"),
  screened = c(410, 455, 380, 362)
)

Make it wide, with one row per district and one column per round.
blocks.answer:
long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = round, values_from = screened)
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  district    r1    r2
  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 Durg       410   455
2 Korba      380   362

Two rows and three columns: Durg screened 410 and 455; Korba 380 and 362.

blocks.prompt:
Two made-up tables:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3), weight_kg = c(60, 72, 55))
y <- tibble(id = c(2, 3, 3, 4), ward = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

Before you run left_join(x, y, by = "id"), say how many rows the result will have and which ward each row gets. Then run it.
blocks.answer:
left_join(x, y, by = "id")
# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id weight_kg ward
  <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>
1     1        60 <NA>
2     2        72 A
3     3        55 B
4     3        55 C

Four rows. Id 1 has no match, so it stays once with NA for ward. Id 2 matches once, ward A. Id 3 matches two rows of y, so it appears twice, with wards B and C. Id 4 is only in y, and a left join keeps only the rows of x. Three rows went in; four came out.

blocks.prompt:
Read the two NHANES files.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

Check that SEQN identifies one row in each file: count how many values of SEQN appear more than once in each.
blocks.answer:
bmx |>
  count(SEQN) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()

demo |>
  count(SEQN) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
[1] 0
[1] 0

0 in each. No participant number repeats in either file, so a join on SEQN cannot add rows.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tidyr)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Make a table with one row per species and one column per island, holding the number of rows of each species on each island. Put 0 where a species was not found on an island, and say why that is the right value here.
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  count(Species, Island) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Island,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  Species                                   Biscoe Dream Torgersen
  <chr>                                      <int> <int>     <int>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)           44    56        52
2 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)      0    68         0
3 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)            124     0         0

Three species, three islands. Adelie penguins were found on all three; Chinstrap only on Dream; Gentoo only on Biscoe. Without values_fill = 0, an island where a species was never recorded would show NA. Here 0 is right: the count of rows for that pair is truly zero, not unknown. In a table of weights, filling a gap with 0 would be wrong, because a missing weight is not a weight of zero.

blocks.prompt:
Read the two NHANES files.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

Join the age column RIDAGEYR to the body measures file. Then count how many examined participants are children under 2, and how many of those have a standing height (BMXHT). Say why the second count is what it is. The BMX codebook lists the ages at which each body measure is taken.
blocks.answer:
body <- bmx |>
  left_join(
    demo |> select(SEQN, RIDAGEYR),
    by = "SEQN",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

body |>
  filter(RIDAGEYR < 2) |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_height = sum(!is.na(BMXHT))
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_rows n_height
   <int>    <int>
1    249        0

The join keeps all 8860 rows. Of the 249 examined participants under 2, none has a standing height. The survey’s documentation lists standing height for ages 2 years and older. Recumbent length, measured lying down, is taken from birth through 47 months, in its own column. So standing height is missing on purpose. A missing value can be part of how the survey works, not a failure to measure.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants one tidy column of penguin measurements. He writes this, and reports “the mean measurement of Gentoo penguins is 1780”.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(tidyr)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Culmen Length (mm)`, `Flipper Length (mm)`, `Body Mass (g)`),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  summarise(mean_value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = Species)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Species                                   mean_value
  <chr>                                          <dbl>
1 Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)            1310.
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)              1780.
3 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)      1326.

Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
The three folded columns are three different variables, in two units: two lengths in millimetres and a mass in grams. The mean of the value column adds grams to millimetres. The number is meaningless, and the large body masses swamp the lengths.

Keep measure in the grouping, so each mean is of one variable in one unit:

penguins_raw |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Culmen Length (mm)`, `Flipper Length (mm)`, `Body Mass (g)`),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  summarise(mean_value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(Species, measure)) |>
  filter(Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)")
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Species                           measure             mean_value
  <chr>                             <chr>                    <dbl>
1 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) Culmen Length (mm)        47.5
2 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) Flipper Length (mm)      217.
3 Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) Body Mass (g)           5076.

Three means for Gentoo penguins, each with its unit in the measure’s name.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: pivot_longer() ran without complaint and the result looked tidy. But a tidy column holds one variable. These three were never one variable, so folding them made the data less tidy, not more.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up clinic keeps two tables. In visits, year is the year of the visit. In register, year is the year of birth. A colleague joins them and reports “no patient’s sex is recorded”.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

visits <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3), year = c(2025, 2025, 2026), bmi = c(26.2, 31.0, 23.4))
register <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3), year = c(1980, 1972, 1991), sex = c("F", "M", "F"))

visits |>
  left_join(register)
Joining with `by = join_by(id, year)`
# A tibble: 3 × 4
     id  year   bmi sex
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
1     1  2025  26.2 <NA>
2     2  2025  31   <NA>
3     3  2026  23.4 <NA>

Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
No by was given, so the join matched on every column the two tables share: id and year. The message says so: it joined by id and year. A visit in 2025 never matches a birth in 1980, so no row found a partner, and sex is NA everywhere.

Name the key:

visits |>
  left_join(register, by = "id")
# A tibble: 3 × 5
     id year.x   bmi year.y sex
  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>
1     1   2025  26.2   1980 F
2     2   2025  31     1972 M
3     3   2026  23.4   1991 F

Now each visit gets its patient’s sex. The two year columns are both kept, and the join adds .x and .y to their names to tell them apart. Rename them to what they mean, such as visit_year and birth_year.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: “sex is not recorded” is a common problem in real registers, so the colleague believed it. The message naming both columns was the clue.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague joins a made-up laboratory table to a register. The laboratory file was read with every column as text.

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

register <- tibble(id = c(101, 102, 103), sex = c("F", "M", "F"))
lab <- tibble(id = c("101", "102", "103"), hb = c("12.1", "14.3", "11.8"))
register |>
  left_join(lab, by = "id")
Error in `left_join()`:
! Can't join `x$id` with `y$id` due to incompatible types.
ℹ `x$id` is a <double>.
ℹ `y$id` is a <character>.

Read the error. Say what broke and fix it.
blocks.answer:
The key is a number in register and text in lab. R will not match 101 with "101", because the two columns have different types. Convert in code, in a new column or by re-reading the file with its column types stated, never by editing the file:

lab_clean <- lab |>
  mutate(id = as.numeric(id), hb = as.numeric(hb))

register |>
  left_join(lab_clean, by = "id")
# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id sex      hb
  <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
1   101 F      12.1
2   102 M      14.3
3   103 F      11.8

Three rows, each with its haemoglobin. The stopping error was the helpful case. Two text columns that differ in another way, such as IDs with and without a leading zero typed as text, would join without error. They would fail to match, and nothing would say so.

Why the wrong code looks reasonable: the two IDs print the same. The type is only visible in the column heading, <dbl> against <chr>.

blocks.prompt: A made-up methods section says: “We merged the NHANES 2021–2023 body measures and demographic files on the sequence number; 11,933 participants had body measures.” Check the claim, and say what the merge does not establish.
blocks.answer:
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

nrow(demo)
nrow(bmx)

bmx |>
  left_join(demo, by = "SEQN", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  nrow()
[1] 11933
[1] 8860
[1] 8860

11933 is the number of rows in the demographics file. It is not the number with body measures. 8860 participants have a body measures record, and the merged file has 8860 rows. The other 3073 were interviewed and not examined. The sentence took the wrong file’s count, which is what happens when the count is read off a screen rather than printed after the join.

What it does not establish:

  • That the 8860 have every measurement. Height, weight and BMI each have missing values, and each analysis has its own n.
  • Anything about the US population. The counts are rows of the files; estimates need the survey’s sample weights.

blocks.prompt: In a made-up journal club, someone says: “In NHANES, women have a higher BMI than men.” Turn the sentence into code on the joined files, for adults aged 20 or over, run it, and say what the result does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Join, keep adults, and summarise BMI by RIAGENDR, where the codebook says 1 is male and 2 is female:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

bmx |>
  left_join(demo, by = "SEQN", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) |>
  summarise(
    n_bmi = sum(!is.na(BMXBMI)),
    mean_bmi = mean(BMXBMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_bmi = median(BMXBMI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = RIAGENDR
  )
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  RIAGENDR n_bmi mean_bmi median_bmi
     <dbl> <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>
1        1  2680     29.3       28.1
2        2  3290     30.3       28.7

In these rows, the 3290 women have a mean BMI of 30.3 kg/m2, and the 2680 men 29.3 kg/m2. The medians are 28.7 and 28.1 kg/m2. So the women examined have a higher mean and median BMI than the men examined.

What it does not establish:

  • That women in the United States have a higher BMI than men. These summaries are unweighted. The survey’s documentation says its sample weights should be used, and the weighted answer could differ.
  • That a difference of about one unit matters, or is more than chance. That needs the statistics books.
  • Anything about body fat. BMI is weight for height; it does not measure body fat.
